title: Working app prototypes that engineering builds from
subtitle: I hand engineering prototypes that already run, on real data. 64% of the code behind the redesigned Home and detail views of the Bibel TV Android app (release 6.0, in beta) comes verbatim from my prototype; for the design system and tokens it is 95–100%.

card.title: Code prototypes as the design-to-engineering handoff
card.line: Prototypes run on real data, so engineering builds from working code instead of specs.

team: Solo design function; product manager and product owner for the redesign. Hamburg / Berlin

sections.headline: Working app prototypes that engineering builds from
sections.subtext: For the Bibel TV app redesign I prototype in real code, against real data, and against APIs I set up myself where the production API didn't carry the data yet. What reaches engineering is an app that already runs. A code comparison measures how much of it they build from.

sections.headline: Engineering builds the redesigned Android Home and detail views from my prototype

metrics.label: The setting
metrics.value: The redesign of the Bibel TV streaming app, iOS and Android. I'm Head of Product Design and, for the redesign, the reason my contract exists, also its product manager and product owner.

metrics.label: My part
metrics.value: I set the direction in Figma, then prototype in Claude Code against real data: web first, then the same prototype continued as a native Kotlin and Jetpack Compose app. Users and stakeholders give feedback by using the working app.

metrics.label: What changed
metrics.value: 64% of the code behind the redesigned Home and detail views of the Bibel TV Android app (release 6.0, in beta) comes verbatim from my prototype; for the design system and tokens it is 95–100%. Measured by code comparison against release 6.0.8, a lower bound. A separate teardown of a pre-release 6.0.2 build found 93.1% of the design-token field names.

metrics.label: Three takeaways
metrics.value: Build the prototype where the largest share of your users are. Hand over something that runs on real data. Leave the build to engineering, and measure what survives.

sections.headline: Two card treatments, the same real episodes
sections.content:
On the Home screen of ProtoBible, my Android prototype, two rows show the same Bibel TV episodes. One row uses one card treatment, the second row another. The episodes are real, loaded from Bibel TV's own content.

So the choice between the two cards gets made on what actually renders. A mockup would have shown each card at its best.

images.alt: Two screens of ProtoBible, the native Android prototype. Left: a verse-of-the-day card on a blue page tinted from the card. Right: Home with the same real episodes shown as two rows of cards, labeled 'Kürzlich overlay' and 'Kürzlich Split'.
images.caption: ProtoBible, the Kotlin and Jetpack Compose prototype, running on real Bibel TV episodes. The rows put two card treatments side by side on the same content, so the choice is made on what renders, not on a mockup. Captured on an emulator from the October 2026 debug build.

sections.headline: A spec leaves the rendering for later
sections.content:
A spec and its redlines describe a screen. The interaction states and the actual rendering get discovered later, by whoever builds it, once a build exists.

That gap costs the most when the people building sit in another company. Every open question becomes an interpretation made by people you don't sit with.

sections.headline: The build used to sit outside the company
sections.content:
Almost all of Bibel TV's development used to depend on an external development agency, so the handoff from design to build crossed a company boundary. Bibel TV has no in-house designers or developers.

That has shifted. Far more is now built in-house, most of the backend and some front-end, by product managers and product owners building with AI. The redesign's Android build is engineering's work, and it builds on my prototype code.

sections.headline: The prototype became the handoff
sections.content:
I still start in Figma, with layout, flow and hierarchy. Exploring design directions stays manual work, by choice: the direction had to be my own judgment, in line with the new on-air brand.

Once the direction is set, I switch to Claude Code and prototype the interfaces with real data. That surfaced issues and edge cases we would not have found in Figma alone. Where the production API didn't carry the data yet, I set up custom APIs so the prototype could still run on real data.

sections.headline: The prototype moved to Android, where the largest part of the users are
sections.content:
The web prototype came first. Mobile browser interfaces have a lot of browser chrome, and the gradient-heavy interface had to be checked against older Android devices prone to banding. A stakeholder had raised that worry: old Android screens in the userbase render gradients badly.

So I continued the same prototype as an Android app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. Android was the right place to build anyway. It is the largest part of the Bibel TV userbase.

Both versions let users and stakeholders give feedback by actually using the app, which a presentation can't offer.

sections.headline: From concept to engineering's build, in five steps
sections.content: Direction first, then the real thing on real data, then the device the users have.

steps.label: Concept in Figma
steps.description: Layout, flow and hierarchy, before any code exists. Exploring design directions stays manual, by choice.

steps.label: Prototype in Claude Code, against real data
steps.description: A working build against the real Bibel TV API, or against a custom API I set up where the production API doesn't carry the data yet.

steps.label: Test on the device that matters
steps.description: The web prototype continued as native Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.

steps.label: Sessions on the working app
steps.description: Users and stakeholders use the app instead of watching a presentation of it.

steps.label: Engineering builds from it
steps.description: Engineering took over the look and built its own data access, view logic and navigation. The code comparison below measures how much of the prototype stayed.

sections.headline: Measured, two ways: how much of the prototype is in the app

metrics.label: What engineering receives
metrics.before: A spec and redlines to interpret
metrics.after: A working prototype, already running against real data

metrics.label: Design-token fields found in the pre-release 6.0.2 Android build
metrics.value: 93.1% of token field names (353 of 379), 94% of the Kotlin token model (443 of 473), confirmed via a teardown of a pre-release build

metrics.label: Prototype code in the redesigned Android views, by code comparison
metrics.value: 64% of the code behind the redesigned Home and detail views of the Android app (release 6.0, in beta) comes verbatim from my prototype; 95–100% for the design system and tokens. A lower bound: code engineering adapted or renamed is not counted

sections.narrative:
Release 6.0 is in beta, so this measures how the redesign is being built. It isn't a consumer number. Two methods answer how much of what I hand over survives. A teardown of a pre-release 6.0.2 build checked the design tokens and data contracts field by field, but it can't see component code. A code comparison of my prototype against release 6.0.8 can: it counts verbatim blocks of Kotlin in the redesigned Home and detail views.

Run against the previous app version, 5.15.5, the same comparison matches 0.03%. The matches with 6.0 are copies, not coincidence. By layer, the design system and tokens carry over at 95–100%, while screen frames and view logic, at 2–3%, are engineering's own.

images.alt: Two bars, measured by code comparison against release 6.0.8. 64% of the code behind the redesigned Home and detail views of the Android app (release 6.0, in beta) comes verbatim from the prototype; 95 to 100% for the design system and tokens.
images.caption: Two shares from one code comparison, kept apart from the teardown figures.

images.alt: Two bars, from a teardown of the pre-release 6.0.2 build. 353 of 379 token field names (93.1%) and 443 of 473 of the Kotlin token model (94%).
images.caption: A separate measurement by a different method: a teardown of a pre-release 6.0.2 build, which checks tokens and data contracts but cannot see component code.

images.alt: Two video detail pages side by side. Left, the prototype: a sermon episode on a warm peach page. Right, Bibel TV's Android app 6.0.7: an episode of The Chosen on a peach page with the same structure of breadcrumb, title, Play button, action row, description and Bible-verse section.
images.caption: Left: the video detail page in the prototype, whose detail redesign I committed on June 12, 2026 and its Bible-verse section on June 18. Right: the same page in the 6.0.7 build of the Bibel TV Android app, October 1, 2026. Same structure; the figures above come from a teardown of the earlier 6.0.2 build and a code comparison against release 6.0.8, not from how alike they look.

sections.headline: The banding came from old displays, not from Android
sections.content:
The stakeholder's worry was about old Android screens. Testing showed the banding is specific to old displays, whatever the platform. That is why the redesign uses multi-step gradients, monochrome ones included.

The question arrived as a hypothesis about a platform, and the running prototype got to correct it.

steps.label: Build the prototype where the largest share of your users are.
steps.description: Pick the platform by your userbase, not by which tooling is fastest. If a stakeholder names a device worry, test it on that device; the finding may be broader than the worry.

steps.label: Hand over something that runs on real data.
steps.description: If the production data doesn't exist yet, set up the smallest API that makes a session honest. Then watch people use the app instead of presenting it to them.

steps.label: Leave the build to engineering, and measure what survives.
steps.description: A code comparison with a control run against the old version gives you a share with a method. Count only verbatim code, and call the result a lower bound.

sections.headline: A prototype can't answer a question that lives in the codebase
sections.content: If the hard part of a project is a migration or a data model, a designed prototype answers none of it. And where engineers sit beside you and review work every day, a formal prototype handoff may cost more than the conversation it replaces.
Two things from this project are worth a call if your handoff crosses a company boundary too: what the 0.03% control run proved, and why the prototype moved from the browser to Kotlin. Get in touch.

A separate teardown of a pre-release 6.0.2 build found 93.1% of the design-token field names and 94% of the Kotlin token model.
